description: We are a team of young innovators participating in the NASA Space Apps Challenge 2026, exploring the fascinating stories behind abandoned NASA equipment on the Moon and Mars. Through research, creativity, and digital storytelling, our team aims to bring these forgotten objects back into the spotlight, uncovering their history, purpose, and contribution to space exploration. Our mission is to show that even when equipment is left behind, its story is never forgotten!
summary:
We made a presentation about the Apollo Lunar Module 10 (Snoopy), it was made to be sent 
from a mothership from Earth to the Moon, it had two compartments and it held two astronauts. 
Once it carried out its mission the top half took the two astronauts to the mothership and went 
back to Earth while the bottom half stayed abandoned at the surface of the moon. We made a 
presentation about this spacecraft in a short video.
details: On June 6, 1968: the Grumman Aircraft Engineering Corporation in Bethpage made the Apollo 10 Lunar Module (also known as Snoopy). It was first launched into space on May 18, 1969. It was light weight and could hold two passengers. It was launched from a mother ship and landed on the Moon’s surface. It had two compartments: One compartment contained the passenger astronauts (Thomas Stafford and Eugene Cernam) inside and served as a ‘mini-space ship’ that took them back to the mother ship when their mission on the moon was complete, and the bottom compartment had spider-like legs that crashed on the lunar surface. Inside the top compartment, there were no seats, so the astronauts had to stand side-by-side and secured by cables and harnesses and looked out of triangular windows. The module wasn’t aerodynamic, so it carried the crew from the mothership down about 9 miles (14.5 km) before crashing to the moon. Snoopy was thermally insulated, the gold material wrapped around it was aluminized Kapton. It was lightweight and its purpose was to reflect solar radiation and protect the spacecraft’s system from extreme temperature swings in space.
